name: PSL scale

lead: PSL, short for Perceived Sexual Levels, is an informal scale looksmaxxing communities use to rate male faces, usually from 1 to 8. It gives members a common benchmark and a target to aim for when they change skin, hair, leanness or style.

It sets out tiers from below average through normie and Chadlite up to Chad and beyond. Raters judge faces on features grouped under harmony, dimorphism, angularity and individual features. Its name is said to combine three forums where it arose, and no published study has evaluated the scale itself.

paras: People post photos for ratings, note their tier, then repost after changes such as a haircut, clearer skin or fat loss to see how opinions shift. Because raters differ, many collect several opinions.

The scale carries no physical risk. It is subjective and not scientifically validated, and commentators cited by Wikipedia link the surrounding culture of tiering people to body dysmorphia and distress.

angle.text: Community members use the PSL scale as a shared yardstick to rate male faces and to measure progress from changes such as skin, hair or leanness. The rating gives a concrete target to work toward, and it reflects community opinion rather than a validated measure.

lead: The PSL scale, short for Perceived Sexual Levels, is an informal system for rating male facial attractiveness on a range of roughly 1 to 8. In looksmaxxing communities it works as a shared yardstick for self-improvement: a member posts photos, receives a rating and a list of features that held the score down, such as skin, jawline, eye area or body fat, and works on those features so that a later rating comes out higher. [1]

Wikipedia reports that the scale was created on three forums, PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, whose initials form the acronym; those sites are now defunct, but the scale and its vocabulary moved to looksmax.org, Reddit and, from the early 2020s, TikTok and live-streaming, largely through male content creators. The scale covers the face only, unlike an ordinary out-of-ten rating of a whole person, and was designed to reflect how women perceive men. [1]

Its tier names, including 'normie', 'Chadlite', 'Chad' and 'subhuman', are among the most widely used terms in looksmaxxing, and rating threads are one of the most common post types on the forums. [1][2][3] Academic researchers have analysed the community's rating boards, and journalists and commentators have covered the scale, often critically. Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, describes the scale as based on harmony, dimorphism, angularity and individual features, and as not scientifically validated. [4] No published study has tested the scale's own scoring against independent ratings, although facial attractiveness is studied widely in psychology. [1]

paras: Wikipedia describes the scale as hierarchical and systematic, designed to interpret how women perceive men, and strictly based on looks. One account in the article lists seven categories: 'subhuman' or sub-3, low-tier, mid-tier and high-tier 'normie', 'Chadlite', 'Chad' and 'giga Chad'. Another account, describing the streamer Braden Peters (Clavicular), uses three tiers: subhuman, normie and Chad. Wikipedia notes that the sources are not consistent about the tiers. [1]

Grokipedia lists below 4 as 'subhuman/truecel', 4.0 to 5.5 as low to high 'normie', 5.6 to 6.5 as 'Chadlite', 6.6 to 7.5 as 'Chad' and 7.6 to 8 as 'Gigachad', and says most men rate around 3.5 to 4.5.

A qualitative study of looksmaxxing forum comments (Halpin and colleagues, 2025) reports that users treat PSL as an objective measure of attractiveness, call the top-rated men 'Chads' and those just below them 'Chadlites', regard men in the middle of the range as 'normies', and describe men rated around 3 or lower as 'subhuman'. [4]

On looksmax.org, members post tier lists that place well-known actors and models at fractional levels such as 6.25 or 6.75, each paired with an estimated rarity in the population (for example 'one in 4,000' for a 6, or 'one in 68' for a 5). Commenters in the thread ask where particular people belong and note that someone whose angularity varies is hard to place. [2]

Wikipedia states that the PSL scale originated on PUAHate.com, Sluthate.com and Lookism.net, which together were called the 'PSL forums', with the wider group known as the 'PSL community'. It gives no founding dates for the sites, and the sites are no longer online. [1]

The same article says that the term 'looksmaxxing' was coined on incel message boards in the 2010s and was popularised on TikTok by mostly male creators in the 2020s, carrying the PSL vocabulary with it. Wikipedia lists press coverage of the phenomenon from Vice in 2018 (on incel forums where members critiqued each other's faces) through Business Insider, the Daily Dot, CBS Baltimore and The New York Times in November 2023, The Guardian and BBC in 2024, and The New York Times and The Guardian profiles of Clavicular in February 2026. [1]

Researchers who studied the incel forum incels.is (a different site) describe the wider 'black pill' belief system, in which women's mate choices are held to be set by looks. That study did not mention the PSL scale itself, but it documents the surrounding ideas of lookism and ranking by category. [5] Wikipedia's article on incels describes the black pill as a belief that dating outcomes are determined largely by genetics and appearance. [6]

Wikipedia also reports that Clavicular, a Kick live-streamer, promotes the PSL scale in interviews and social-media posts, and that scholars including Solea and Sugiura (2025) have written on the scale and its 'digital subcultural diffusion'. [1]

sections.h: What the scale is said to measure
paras: Wikipedia says that people judging a man's attractiveness on this scale usually check a set of facial features, and it lists 'hunter eyes' (a positive canthal tilt with little upper eyelid showing and low-set brows), hollow cheeks, a defined jawline and 'pursed lips' among them. [1] Grokipedia groups the criteria as harmony, dimorphism, angularity and individual features.

Forum members extend the numbers into a wider idea of 'sexual market value' (SMV), in which a facial rating is combined with perceived status and wealth. [1] Halpin and colleagues describe users measuring each other's faces and bodies against masculine ideals such as jaw, brow, height and musculature, and note that the community favours a 'goldilocks' level of intervention, with too much seen as unmasculine. [4]

Rating threads are a staple of the forums. A typical post gives height, a short self-description and photos and asks for a PSL rating plus advice; one thread author mentions considering isotretinoin for acne and asks what to improve. [3] Another member says he is planning lower jaw surgery and asks for a rating and a list of improvements. [7]

In the study of 8,072 comments from a self-improvement board and a ratings board, the authors found that practices discussed alongside ratings included mewing, bonesmashing talk, leg-lengthening surgery and cosmetic procedures. [4]
Wikipedia describes looksmaxxers asking others to rate their appearance, with the rating sometimes combined with perceived status and wealth into SMV. [1]

Members discuss how other traits convert into PSL points. In one thread a user asks how many inches of height equal two to three PSL points; a reply says height is not very influential, perhaps one point, and that facial beauty and a decent physique matter more. [8]

Looksmax.org users also debate how PSL differs from 'appeal'. One thread author says common explanations equate PSL with male-gaze features and appeal with female-gaze harmony and social factors, while noting that long-time members dispute this framing.  Other threads argue the scale reflects the female gaze imperfectly or that women sort men into a few coarse categories. [9][10]

The PSL scale has not been examined in published research as a measurement instrument, but the properties it names overlap with topics studied in psychology. Wikipedia's overview of physical attractiveness reports computer-averaging studies in which averaged faces were rated more attractive, studies linking facial symmetry to attractiveness in both sexes, and work on women's preferences for masculine facial dimorphism that varies with menstrual cycle phase, self-rated attractiveness and country. [11]

The same overview describes cross-cultural work by Cunningham (1995) with East Asian, Hispanic, White and African American judges, which found broad agreement about which faces are attractive. [11] The wider literature on appearance bias, summarised in Wikipedia's article on lookism, reports that attractive people are perceived somewhat more positively and have received more callbacks in several field experiments of hiring. [12]
These studies concern general attractiveness ratings and do not test the PSL tiers or numbers.

Halpin, Gosse, Yeo, Handlovsky and Maguire (Sociology of Health & Illness, 2025) analysed 8,072 comments collected in 2023 from a looksmaxxing website, 5,327 from a self-improvement board and 2,745 from a ratings board, sampling threads with at least 100 replies. They report that users rate one another on the PSL scale, treat the numbers as objective, and rank men of colour with racial caricatures. They also report that the community often treats men who fall short as failed men, and they document many instances of users encouraging others to die by suicide and some users expressing suicidal thoughts themselves. They argue that looksmaxxing affects men's health and propose revising Courtenay's theory of men's health to account for masculinity motivating medical interventions. [4]
The authors acknowledge limits: comments are assumed authentic, no demographic data were available, and photos were not analysed. [4]

Wikipedia reports commentators describing looksmaxxing as judgmental and harmful, linking rating cultures to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, and describing the PSL scale as pseudoscientific. It quotes New Yorker writer Becca Rothfeld (7 March 2026) objecting to any system that designates a person as 'subhuman', and records The Conversation's Rosdahl (January 2024) warning that looksmaxxing can lead young men toward incel views. [1]
The same article notes that some practitioners report benefits such as improved health habits and relationships. [1]

On the forums themselves, members criticise the scale from the inside: one thread argues PSL is flawed at its core because women put men into a handful of categories, [10] and another argues the scale is detached from reality and from the female gaze. [9]
No studies found that validate the PSL scale. Research on facial attractiveness exists in the wider psychology literature but does not test this scale. [1][11]

lore.intro: PSL is core vocabulary on looksmax.org, where users rate faces, publish celebrity tier lists and argue over what the scale measures. [2]

claims.claim: PSL measures facial attractiveness as women perceive it.
PSL and appeal are different things.
Height is worth about one PSL point.
The scale is an objective measure of a man's looks.
Women sort men into a few coarse categories, so fine-grained PSL numbers matter less.
Faces that rate highly share features such as angularity, dimorphism and harmony.
Rating the face is a road to improving it.

timeline.event: Scale originates on the PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net forums. [1]
Vice reports on incel forums where members critique each other's faces. [1]
Looksmaxxing and its rating vocabulary appear in TikTok-focused coverage from Business Insider, the Daily Dot and The New York Times (November). [1]
The Conversation (January), The Guardian (February) and the BBC (March) publish overviews of looksmaxxing. [1]
Halpin and colleagues publish a qualitative analysis of 8,072 looksmaxxing forum comments, including the PSL scale. [4]
The New York Times and The Guardian profile Clavicular (February); Rothfeld criticises the scale in The New Yorker (7 March). [1]
